{
  "hypothesis": "Predicted that the framing of the dictator game (giving vs. taking) would have asymmetric effects on the allocation behavior of male and female dictators, specifically that males would be more selfish in the taking frame compared to the giving frame, while females would be more egalitarian in the taking frame compared to the giving frame.",
  "design": "between, two conditions (giving frame vs. taking frame)",
  "manipulation_or_predictor": "The framing of the dictator game: in the 'giving' frame, the dictator decides how much of their £10 to give to the recipient; in the 'taking' frame, the recipient has the £10 and the dictator decides how much to take for themselves.",
  "outcome_measure": "The amount of money allocated to the recipient (in the giving frame, the amount given; in the taking frame, £10 minus the amount taken).",
  "population_and_setting": "Students at the University of East Anglia, recruited via ORSEE, participating in a computerized laboratory experiment.",
  "sample_size_total": 140,
  "recruitment_and_incentive": "Recruited via ORSEE; all subjects received a £3 show-up fee. Dictators made a decision regarding a £10 fund.",
  "analysis_plan": "Mann-Whitney tests and OLS regressions comparing allocations between frames, split by gender, and Probit models to analyze the likelihood of 'selfish' (allocating 0) or 'egalitarian' (allocating half) behavior.",
  "preregistered_or_confirmatory": "not stated",
  "other_methods_notes": "The study used a balanced pool of 35 male and 35 female dictators per treatment (total 280 participants, but only 140 dictators). The roles of dictator and recipient were passive and anonymous. Neutral language ('transfer', 'access') was used to minimize experimenter demand effects."
}
